## Learning Objectives

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
- Orthogonal projection onto a vector
- Orthogonal projection onto a subspace
    - Properties: closest point and distance
- Gram-Schmidt process
    - Two perspectives
    - Creating an orthogonal basis from any basis
:::

:::{style="font-size: .75em"}
_Recall from L22: orthogonal bases make coordinates easy to compute. Today we'll see they also make projection easy._
:::

## Projection: The Core of Prediction{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .85em"}
Recall the central question from L20: our housing price vector $\mathbf{b}$ is almost certainly **not** in $\operatorname{Col} A$.

But we can still find the **closest** vector in $\operatorname{Col} A$ to $\mathbf{b}$ — the best possible prediction given our model. That closest vector is the **orthogonal projection** of $\mathbf{b}$ onto $\operatorname{Col} A$.

This single geometric idea is the foundation of:

- **Least squares** (L25): the projection is exactly $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, the fitted values
- **Residuals**: $\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is the component of $\mathbf{b}$ orthogonal to $\operatorname{Col} A$ — the irreducible prediction error
- **Linear regression** (L26): minimizing $\|\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\|^2$ is the same as projecting $\mathbf{b}$ onto $\operatorname{Col} A$

Today we derive projection and learn Gram-Schmidt, which gives us the orthogonal bases that make projection efficient.
:::

## Decomposing a Vector: Projection and Remainder{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
:::{.center-text}
```{python}
import laUtilities as ut
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

ax = ut.plotSetup(-1,10,-1,4,(7,4))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
pt = [4., 3.]
plt.plot([0,pt[0]],[0,pt[1]],'b-',lw=2)
plt.plot([0,2*pt[0]],[0,0],'r-',lw=3)
ut.plotVec(ax,pt,'b')
u = np.array([pt[0],0])
ut.plotVec(ax,2*u)
ax.text(2*pt[0],-0.75,r'$\mathbf{u}$',size=20)
ax.text(pt[0]+0.1,pt[1]+0.2,r'$\mathbf{y}$',size=20);
```
:::
Suppose we have nonzero vectors $\mathbf{y}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The goal of projection is to "decompose" $\mathbf{y}$ into the sum of two vectors $\mathbf{y} = \hat{\mathbf{y}} + \mathbf{z}$ such that

- $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the __orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $\mathbf{u}$__: $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \alpha\mathbf{u}$ for some scalar $\alpha$.

- $\mathbf{z}$ is the __component of $\mathbf{y}$ orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$__: it is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$.
:::

## Geometric View of Projection{.really-smaller-title}

:::{.center-text}

## Deriving the Projection Formula{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Note $\mathbf{y} - \alpha\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{z}.$ We want $\mathbf{z}$ to be orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}.$
:::

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Now $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{y} - \alpha{\mathbf{u}}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$ if and only if

$$
\begin{align*}
0 &= (\mathbf{y} - \alpha\mathbf{u})^\top \mathbf{u}\\
&= \mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u} - (\alpha\mathbf{u})^\top \mathbf{u} \\
&= \mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u} - \alpha(\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u}).
\end{align*}
$$

Hence,  $\mathbf{z}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$ happens if and only if $\alpha = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u}}.$

Since $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \alpha\mathbf{u}$,

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}.
$$

:::

```{python}

    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```

## Only Direction Matters: Proof{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
- Geometrically: if we scale $\mathbf{u}$, we do not change the location of $\hat{\mathbf{y}}.$

- Algebraically: replace $\mathbf{u}$ with $c\mathbf{u}$ and recompute $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$: $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^{\top} c\mathbf{u}}{c\mathbf{u}^{\top} c\mathbf{u}}c\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^{\top} \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top} \mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}.$

Therefore, the projection of $\mathbf{y}$ is determined by the __subspace__ $L$ that is spanned by $\mathbf{u},$ the line through $\mathbf{u}$ and the origin.

<br>

Hence, sometimes $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is denoted by $\mbox{proj}_L \mathbf{y}$ and is called the __orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $L$:__

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mbox{proj}_L \mathbf{y} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^{\top} \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top} \mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}.
$$
:::

## Computing a Projection: Example{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .9em"}
__Example__. Let $\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix}7\\6\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix}.$  We are going to write $\mathbf{y}$ as the sum of a vector in Span$\{\mathbf{u}\}$ and a vector orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}.$

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
ax = ut.plotSetup(-3,11,-1,7,(7,5))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
plt.axis('equal')
u = np.array([4.,2])
y = np.array([7.,6])
yhat = (y.T.dot(u)/u.T.dot(u))*u
z = y-yhat
ut.plotLinEqn(1.,-2.,0.)
ut.plotVec(ax,u)
ut.plotVec(ax,z)
ut.plotVec(ax,y)
ut.plotVec(ax,yhat)
ax.text(u[0]+0.3,u[1]-0.5,r'$\mathbf{u}$',size=20)
ax.text(yhat[0]+0.3,yhat[1]-0.5,r'$\mathbf{\hat{y}}$',size=20)
ax.text(y[0],y[1]+0.8,r'$\mathbf{y}$',size=20)
ax.text(z[0]-2,z[1],r'$\mathbf{y - \hat{y}}$',size=20)
ax.text(10,4.5,r'$L = $Span$\{\mathbf{u}\}$',size=20)
perpline1, perpline2 = ut.perp_sym(yhat, y, np.array([0,0]), 0.75)
plt.plot(perpline1[0], perpline1[1], 'k', lw = 1)
plt.plot(perpline2[0], perpline2[1], 'k', lw = 1)
ax.plot([y[0],yhat[0]],[y[1],yhat[1]],'b--')
ax.plot([0,y[0]],[0,y[1]],'b-')
ax.plot([0,z[0]],[0,z[1]],'b-');
```
:::
:::

## Computing a Projection: Inner Products{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
First, we compute the inner products:

$$
\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix}7&6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix} = 40,
$$

$$
\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix}4&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix} = 20.
$$

The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $\mathbf{u}$ is

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u}} \mathbf{u}
$$

$$
=\frac{40}{20}\mathbf{u} = 2\begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}8\\4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:::

## Verifying the Components Are Orthogonal{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
The component of $\small \mathbf{y}$ orthogonal to $\small \mathbf{u}$ is

$$ \small
\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \begin{bmatrix}7\\6\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix}8\\4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We can write
$$ \small
\begin{array}{ccccc}
\mathbf{y} &=& \hat{\mathbf{y}} &+& \mathbf{z}. \\
\begin{bmatrix}7\\6\end{bmatrix} &=& \begin{bmatrix}8\\4\end{bmatrix} &+& \begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\end{bmatrix}
\end{array}.
$$

Furthermore, $\small \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ and $\small \mathbf{z}$ are orthogonal. We can quickly check this for ourselves using the inner product:

$$\small
\hat{\mathbf{y}}^\top \mathbf{z} = 8(-1) + 4(2) = -8 + 8 = 0.
$$
:::

## Projection Is the Closest Point in the Subspace{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

**1.** _The closest point._

Recall from geometry that given a line and a point $P$, the closest point on the line to $P$ is given by the perpendicular from $P$ to the line.

Hence, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is __the closest point to $\mathbf{y}$ in the subspace $L$.__

:::{.center-text}

## Distance from a Point to a Subspace{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
**2.** _The distance from $\mathbf{y}$ to $L$_

The distance from $\mathbf{y}$ to $L$ is the length of the perpendicular from $\mathbf{y}$ to its orthogonal projection on $L$, namely $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$.

This distance equals the length of $\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$, or in other words the norm of ${\bf z}$.

In the previous example, the distance is

$$
\Vert\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}\Vert = \Vert {\bf z} \Vert = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5}.
$$

:::

```{python}

    return r"""

        <p>How would you use projection to compute the distance from a point \(\mathbf{y}\) to a plane through the origin?</p>
    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```

## The Gram-Schmidt Algorithm{.smaller-title}

The __Gram-Schmidt process__ is an algorithm that transforms a basis $\{ {\bf v}_1, {\bf v}_2, \ldots, {\bf v}_n \}$ for subspace $H$ into an orthogonal basis $\{ {\bf u}_1, {\bf u}_2, \ldots, {\bf u}_n \}$ for the same subspace $H$. It operates as follows.

$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
{\bf u}_1 &=& {\bf v}_1 \\
{\bf u}_2 &=& {\bf v}_2 - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_1}({\bf v}_2) \\
{\bf u}_3 &=& {\bf v}_3 - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_1}({\bf v}_3) - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_2}({\bf v}_3) \\
&\vdots& \\
{\bf u}_n &=& {\bf v}_n - \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_i}({\bf v}_n)
\end{eqnarray*}
$$

In other words, we can find an orthogonal basis by iteratively removing the projections of all previous vectors, in order to keep only the component of each vector that is orthogonal to all vectors before it.

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>In the Gram-Schmidt process, why must we subtract projections onto <em>all</em> previous orthogonal vectors, not just the first one?</p>
    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```

## Gram-Schmidt: A Geometric Perspective{.smaller-title}

Here is another way to think about the Gram-Schmidt process.

:::{.incremental}
- Set ${\bf u}_1 = {\bf v}_1$.
- Overwrite each of ${\bf v}_2, {\bf v}_3, \ldots, {\bf v}_n$ with the component orthogonal to ${\bf u}_1$.
- Now ${\bf v}_2 \perp {\bf u}_1.$ Set ${\bf u}_2 = {\bf v}_2$.
- Overwrite each of ${\bf v}_3, {\bf v}_4, \ldots, {\bf v}_n$ with the component orthogonal to ${\bf u}_2$.
- Now ${\bf v}_3 \perp {\bf u}_1$ and ${\bf v}_3 \perp {\bf u}_2.$ Set ${\bf u}_3 = {\bf v}_3$.
- Continue until all vectors are processed.
:::

## Warm-Up: Gram-Schmidt in $\mathbb{R}^2${.smaller-title}

```{python}

        <ol type="a">
            <li>Set \(\mathbf{u}_1 = \mathbf{v}_1.\) What is \(\mathbf{u}_1\)?</li>
            <li>Compute \(\mathbf{u}_2 = \mathbf{v}_2 - \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_1}(\mathbf{v}_2).\)</li>
            <li>Verify that \(\mathbf{u}_1 \perp \mathbf{u}_2.\)</li>
        </ol>
        </p>
    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```

:::{.notes}
u₁ = [3,4]ᵀ. proj = (v₂·u₁)/(u₁·u₁) u₁ = (3/25)[3,4]ᵀ = [9/25, 12/25]ᵀ.
u₂ = [1,0]ᵀ − [9/25, 12/25]ᵀ = [16/25, −12/25]ᵀ.
Check: u₁·u₂ = 3(16/25)+4(−12/25) = 48/25−48/25 = 0. ✓
:::

## Gram-Schmidt: Example Setup{.smaller-title}

We are going to apply the Gram-Schmidt process to the following three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ to produce an orthogonal set:

$$
{\bf v_1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
{\bf v_2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
{\bf v_3} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Note that these vectors $\{ {\bf v_1}, {\bf v_2}, {\bf v_3} \}$ do not form an orthogonal set.

For example, ${\bf v}_{\bf 1}^\top {\bf v_2} = 1$, not zero.
<br><br>

The first step of the Gram-Schmidt process is simple: ${\bf u_1} = {\bf v_1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

## Gram-Schmidt: Computing v₂{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .9em"}

Next, we need to calculate only the part of ${\bf v_2}$ that is orthogonal to ${\bf u_1}$.

:::{.fragment}
$$
\begin{align*}
{\bf u_2} &= {\bf v_2} - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u_1}}({\bf v_2}) \\
&= {\bf v_2} - \left(\frac{{\bf v_2}^\top {\bf u_1}}{{\bf u_1}^\top {\bf u_1}}\right) {\bf u_1} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{1}{2} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ -1/2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}
$$

This process guarantees that ${\bf u_2}$ is orthogonal to ${\bf u_1}$. We can check this for ourselves.

$$
{\bf u}_{\bf 1}^\top {\bf u_2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}  \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ -1/2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 1/2 - 1/2 + 0 = 0.
$$
:::
:::

## Gram-Schmidt: Computing v₃{.smaller-title}

Finally, we calculate $\bf{u_3}$:

:::{.fragment}
$$
\begin{align*}
{\bf u}_3 &= {\bf v}_3 - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_1}({\bf v}_3) - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_2}({\bf v}_3) \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{{\bf v_3}^\top {\bf u_1}}{{\bf u_1}^\top {\bf u_1}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{{\bf v_3}^\top {\bf u_2}}{{\bf u_2}^\top {\bf u_2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ -1/2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{1}{2} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{1/2}{3/2} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ -1/2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} -2/3 \\ 2/3 \\ 2/3 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{align*}
$$
:::

## Gram-Schmidt: Verifying the Result{.smaller-title}

We can verify that $\mathbf{u}_3 \perp \mathbf{u}_2$ and $\mathbf{u}_3 \perp \mathbf{u}_1.$

Therefore, $\{ {\bf u_1}, {\bf u_2}, {\bf u_3} \}$ is an orthogonal set.

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
         <p><span class="label">Theorem</span>
        If we apply Gram-Schmidt starting from a basis \(\{ {\bf v}_1, {\bf v}_2, \ldots, {\bf v}_n \}\) for subspace \(H\), then the resulting set \(\mathcal{B} = \{ {\bf u}_1, {\bf u}_2, \ldots, {\bf u}_n \}\) satisfies the following properties:
        <ol start=1>
        <li>The vectors in \(\mathcal{B}\) are orthogonal.</li>
        <li>\(\mathcal{B}\) spans the same subspace \(H\), and hence is a basis for \(H\).</li>
        </ol>
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

## Gram-Schmidt: Before and After{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
The vectors $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ are not orthogonal. Gram-Schmidt produces orthogonal $\{\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2, \mathbf{u}_3\}$ spanning the same subspace.
:::

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D

v1 = np.array([1., 1., 0.])
v2 = np.array([1., 0., 1.])
v3 = np.array([0., 1., 1.])

u1 = np.array([1., 1., 0.])
u2 = np.array([0.5, -0.5, 1.])
u3 = np.array([-2/3, 2/3, 2/3])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 4.5))

for col, (vecs, labels, colors, title) in enumerate([
    ([v1, v2, v3], [r'$\mathbf{v}_1$', r'$\mathbf{v}_2$', r'$\mathbf{v}_3$'],
     ['steelblue', 'darkorange', 'green'], 'Before: original basis\n(not orthogonal)'),
    ([u1, u2, u3], [r'$\mathbf{u}_1$', r'$\mathbf{u}_2$', r'$\mathbf{u}_3$'],
     ['steelblue', 'darkorange', 'green'], 'After: orthogonal basis\n(Gram-Schmidt result)')
]):
    ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, col + 1, projection='3d')
    for v, lbl, clr in zip(vecs, labels, colors):
        ax.quiver(0, 0, 0, v[0], v[1], v[2], color=clr, arrow_length_ratio=0.15, linewidth=2)
        ax.text(v[0]*1.1, v[1]*1.1, v[2]*1.1, lbl, fontsize=13, color=clr, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlim([-1, 1.2]); ax.set_ylim([-1, 1.2]); ax.set_zlim([-0.2, 1.2])
    ax.set_xlabel('x', fontsize=10); ax.set_ylabel('y', fontsize=10); ax.set_zlabel('z', fontsize=10)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11, pad=8)
    ax.view_init(elev=20, azim=35)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

## Gram-Schmidt and Decorrelated Features{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .85em"}
Gram-Schmidt takes any basis and produces an **orthogonal** one spanning the same subspace. In data science terms: it replaces a set of correlated features with an equivalent set of **uncorrelated** ones.

This matters because:

- **Correlated features** cause numerical problems (multicollinearity, unstable coefficients)
- **Orthogonal features** make computation and interpretation much cleaner
- PCA applies Gram-Schmidt-style orthogonalization to the covariance structure of your data, producing "principal components" — the most informative uncorrelated directions

The next step (L24) takes this further: Gram-Schmidt + normalization = **QR decomposition**, the practical engine behind least squares solvers in numpy, scipy, and sklearn.
:::

## Looking Ahead: QR Decomposition{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .85em"}
Gram-Schmidt produces an orthogonal basis — but we can go further.

- If we **normalize** each $\mathbf{u}_i$ to unit length, we get an **orthonormal** basis $\{\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_n\}$.
- Stacking these as columns gives an orthonormal matrix $Q$.
- The original matrix $A = [\mathbf{v}_1 \; \mathbf{v}_2 \; \cdots \; \mathbf{v}_n]$ factors as $A = QR$, where $R$ is upper triangular.

**Next lecture (L24):** We'll derive the QR decomposition and see how it simplifies solving least-squares problems.
:::
